paras: Two years ago, a large cancer hospital in Chicago had a very bad night. At about ten in the evening, the computer system crashed, and it did not come back for six hours. The staff had to work with paper and pens. The nurses had to write every medicine by hand, and the doctors had to call the lab on the phone for every test result.

Nobody was hurt, but the night was very difficult. The hospital had a backup system, but it was in the same building, and it crashed too. There was also a protocol for this situation, but it had twenty pages, and most of the staff did not know it.

After the incident, the director said: "This was not one person's mistake. It was a lesson for all of us." The hospital made three changes. First, the backup system now has to be in a different city. Second, every team has to do a drill twice a year: one hour with paper, like on that night. Third, the training is now required for new nurses and doctors in their first month.

There is also good news for the staff. They don't have to remember the whole protocol now: it is on one page, next to every computer. "We can't prevent every crash," says the director, "but we can prevent the panic."
reading.source: A short story written for this lesson, based on what many hospitals do after a long system crash.

listenings.text: Hi everyone, this is Marcos from IT, with the new downtime protocol. After last month's incident, we had to make some changes. From now on, the backup server has to be in our second building, not in the same room. Every team has to do a one-hour drill, in March and in September. During the drill, you have to use the paper forms, like on the night of the crash. You don't have to print anything: the forms are already at every nurses' station. New staff have to do the training in their first month. It is required, and it takes only forty minutes. One lesson we learned is simple: nobody can prevent every problem, but a good plan prevents the panic. Thank you, and see you at the drill.

Let me tell you about my first mistake at work. It was my first week at a small hospital in Boston, more than twenty years ago. I sent a patient report to the wrong doctor. When I noticed it, I felt terrible, and I was afraid to tell my manager. But I told her, and she was not angry. She said: You don't have to hide a mistake. You have to tell me fast. Then we had to call the other doctor, and we fixed the problem in ten minutes. After that day, the whole team had to use a checklist before they sent any report. That checklist is still there today. For me, that is the best lesson learned: a mistake is information. If you say it early, the team can learn from it.
